2. Implement Spec-Driven Development (SDD): Structure engineering tasks into five sequential stages (specify -> plan -> tasks -> implement -> converge) using tools like GitHub Spec Kit or OpenSpec before generating code.

WHY: Establishes the empirical design foundation required to transition autonomous software development from stochastic, hallucination-prone prompt-and-pray methods into deterministic, verifiable engineering workflows with isolated multi-agent runtimes, formal DoD gates, and structured AST/hybrid retrieval.
WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not rely on single-model prompt roleplay (asking one LLM to pretend to be multiple developers in a single conversational thread) for mission-critical tasks due to prompt leakage and persona degradation. Do not let autonomous agents operate without bounded loops (--max-turns) or financial cost limits. Do not allow agents to run destructive terminal commands or make direct production modifications without git snapshotting/checkpointing and human-in-the-loop review. Relational database baseline: Deploy PostgreSQL (v15+ mandatory due to v14 EOL; 17/18 recommended) for standard transactional workloads; pair with pgvector and pgx-bm25 for unified vector and BM25 search without ancillary search clusters; adopt connection poolers (PgBouncer, Supavisor) for serverless environments.

2. Embedded and edge database deployment: Utilize SQLite (WAL mode enabled) for desktop, mobile, CLI, and integration testing; deploy libSQL/Turso for geo-distributed edge replicas and serverless SQLite.

3. ORM and query builder configuration: Standardize TypeScript monoliths on Prisma (declarative schema.prisma, Studio, Accelerate) or select Drizzle ORM for edge runtimes and high-performance serverless where SQL dialect transparency, low bundle overhead, and native RLS support are required; use Kysely when full SQL expression control with pure TypeScript types is preferred.

4. Vector engine and search implementation: For zero-infrastructure vector search, activate pgvector in PostgreSQL; for dedicated RAG workloads, deploy Qdrant (Rust-native, quantization) or Weaviate (HNSW, generative search modules, GraphQL/gRPC); deploy Meilisearch or Typesense for instant storefront search and typo-tolerant search-as-you-type autocomplete.

5. Cache and key-value broker selection: Deploy Valkey (BSD-3-Clause) as the open-source continuation of Redis for cache/queues, or utilize Upstash (REST API over HTTP) for edge and serverless environments lacking persistent TCP connections.

6. Schema migration and GitOps pipelines: Manage polyglot or JVM database migrations via Flyway versioned scripts (V1__, R__) with validateOnMigrate in CI; adopt Ariga Atlas for declarative HCL/SQL desired-state schemas and automated schema drift checks in pull requests.
WHY: Catalog 04 establishes a comprehensive, audited 2026 architectural reference across data persistence, query abstraction, vector indexing, caching, and database lifecycle tooling. Rapid developments across 2024-2026—including the Redis licensing transition to RSALv2/SSPL resulting in the Valkey fork, PostgreSQL 14 EOL, the maturation of Rust-based vector search engines (Qdrant), native in-database hybrid search (pgvector + pgx-bm25), and declarative GitOps schema migrations (Atlas)—demand rigorous technical evaluation to prevent vendor lock-in, license violations, and architectural anti-patterns.
WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not run PostgreSQL versions prior to 15 in production, as v14 reaches end-of-life (EOL 2026-11-12). Do not adopt Redis in open-source distributions without verifying licensing terms (RSALv2/SSPLv1+AGPLv3 mix); migrate to Valkey (BSD-3-Clause) where strict OSI compliance is mandated. Never expose raw SQLite or DuckDB database files over public web interfaces or execute untrusted DuckDB database files with community autoload enabled without cryptographic verification. Do not bypass input parameterization: parameterize all raw SQL in Drizzle/SQLAlchemy/Kysely and all Cypher queries in Neo4j to prevent injection vulnerabilities. Do not deploy serverless functions connecting directly to PostgreSQL or MySQL without connection pooling (PgBouncer/Supavisor), which exhausts DB connection limits. Do not store sensitive PII in vector embeddings or search indexes without encryption at rest and access policies (RLS/tenant filtering).

HARNESS_WIRING.universal_note: Reference catalog for relational/NoSQL/graph/vector databases, ORMs, migrations, and caching systems (PostgreSQL, SQLite/Turso, Redis/Valkey, MongoDB, Neo4j, Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector, Prisma, Drizzle, SQLAlchemy, Flyway, Atlas, Upstash, S3/MinIO, DuckDB). Serves as an architecture, driver, and ORM selection guide; individual technologies are wired via application connection strings (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL), schema definitions (schema.prisma, drizzle/schema.ts, models.py), and migration configs (flyway.conf, atlas.hcl).

conflicts: Licensing transition and forks: Redis transitioned from BSD-3-Clause to source-available RSALv2/SSPLv1 (plus AGPLv3 dual license), prompting the Linux Foundation Valkey fork; commercial redistributions must distinguish between Redis and Valkey.
PostgreSQL lifecycle: PostgreSQL 14 reaches official EOL on 2026-11-12; production systems must target PostgreSQL 15, 16, 17, or 18.

MongoDB and Elasticsearch licensing: MongoDB SSPL and Elastic License/SSPL are not OSI-approved licenses; managed cloud reselling requires commercial agreements or open-source forks (FerretDB for Mongo wire protocol, OpenSearch for Elasticsearch).

TypeScript ORM paradigms: Prisma uses a domain-specific schema language (schema.prisma) and precompiled query engines, whereas Drizzle and Kysely use pure TypeScript schema definitions and thin SQL query generation, creating distinct trade-offs between schema tooling vs bundle size and serverless cold start times.

SQLite concurrency model: SQLite supports only a single concurrent writer; high-write throughput workloads require distributed replication mechanisms (libSQL/Turso, LiteFS) or migration to client-server RDBMS (PostgreSQL, MySQL).

Do not rely on client-side form validation or headless UI primitives as security boundaries; all inputs and permissions must be validated on the backend. WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not default to headless browser automation (Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium) when target content is accessible via direct HTTP or exposed backend JSON endpoints; browser engines incur a 10x to 50x compute overhead and 2 to 10 second latency per page. 5. 6. Scheduled jobs and edge data: Implement durable background workflows, idempotency keys, and retry pipelines using Trigger.dev or Inngest rather than unmonitored scripts; use pg_cron for database-colocated maintenance; restrict Cloudflare D1 or Turso to read-heavy low-concurrency edge data workloads adhering to strict single-writer SQLite limits (<10GB) while routing write-heavy enterprise schemas to managed PostgreSQL on Render or Neon.
WHY: Provides an audited 2026 reference architecture and comparative evaluation across the modern cloud deployment stack. Resolves fundamental trade-offs between developer experience, operational complexity, vendor lock-in, and infrastructure cost: high-convenience serverless platforms (Vercel, Netlify) incur significant bandwidth and add-on database overheads, whereas cloud primitives (AWS Lambda, S3, CloudFront) provide orders-of-magnitude cost savings at the expense of manual configuration. WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not conflate CI build engines with CD deployment orchestrators (do not script ad-hoc production SSH or kubectl deploy steps inside continuous integration runners; delegate cluster reconciliation to GitOps controllers like Argo CD or Flux). Do not connect ephemeral preview pull-request deployments to production database instances; provision isolated preview database branches via Neon or Supabase to prevent catastrophic data corruption. Do not expose ephemeral preview URLs to search engines or public traffic without access control headers (robots: noindex) or synthetic auth gating. Do not rely on free-tier Render web services for customer-facing production due to severe 15-minute idle spin-down latency, and beware that Render free PostgreSQL databases are automatically deleted after 30 days plus a 14-day grace period. Do not deploy write-heavy relational workloads exceeding 10GB to Cloudflare D1 due to its hard storage ceiling and single-writer concurrency bottlenecks; select managed PostgreSQL instead. Do not grant automated headless deploy agents unrestricted production promotion privileges; enforce human-in-the-loop review gates with short-lived scoped OIDC deploy roles.

HOW_TO_USE: 1. Implement programmatic SEO and structured data: Use Next.js App Router metadataBase to construct absolute Open Graph and Twitter image URLs; generate dynamic sitemaps and robots rules via sitemap.ts and robots.ts; inject Schema.org JSON-LD scripts directly into server components for Product and Article models, dynamically hydrating price and availability from the commerce engine.

Monitor search health and Core Web Vitals: Connect domains to Google Search Console to track crawl deltas and CrUX field vitals; configure Lighthouse CI (lhci) in pull request pipelines to enforce lab budgets (LCP <2.5s, INP <200ms, CLS <0.1); combine with Real User Monitoring (RUM) via Vercel Speed Insights or Sentry to track p75 field regressions.

3. Configure privacy-compliant analytics: Deploy Google Consent Mode v2 or cookieless trackers (Plausible, Matomo); implement CMP prior-blocking (Cookiebot, Didomi, c15t) so marketing tags, ads, and session replays are completely blocked until explicit user consent is granted; verify network requests via proxy inspection to ensure Deny halts all tracking packets.

4. Execute edge-based A/B testing: Utilize GrowthBook or Optimizely with edge middleware or server-side bucketing to evaluate feature flags and variants; set HTTP Vary headers and exclude search bots to eliminate UI flicker and prevent Google cloaking penalties; tie experiment metrics to analytics data warehouses (BigQuery/Snowflake).

5. Architecture rule for headless CMS and commerce (The Reference Pattern): Decouple content from commerce so the CMS (Sanity, Contentful, Strapi) manages only editorial content, marketing layouts, and SEO fields, while the commerce engine (Shopify, Medusa, Saleor) remains the sole authoritative source of truth for products, pricing, inventory, carts, and checkout. Store commerce handles or entity IDs as references in the CMS—never duplicate product pricing or stock levels into CMS records.

6. Caching and invalidation strategy: Cache marketing content aggressively at the edge and invalidate using on-demand webhook revalidation (revalidateTag("sanity") or on-publish webhooks); cache commerce product data with ultra-short TTLs (e.g., 60 seconds) or fetch live at render time for price-sensitive and inventory-critical checkout paths; disable Add to Cart immediately when inventory reaches zero.

7. Secure payment processing and cart validation: Terminate checkout sessions through Stripe Checkout or Stripe Payment Element to preserve SAQ-A PCI compliance; strictly compute cart pricing, taxes, discounts, and order totals on the server backend—never accept client-calculated amounts; verify incoming Stripe webhook signatures (stripe-signature) and process webhook events (checkout.session.completed) idempotently.

8. Wire transactional messaging and growth services: Dispatch transactional notifications (receipts, password resets) via Resend or SendGrid using durable job queues (Trigger.dev, Inngest) with configured SPF/DKIM/DMARC records; handle multi-locale routing via next-intl middleware; synchronize product and editorial catalogs to Algolia or Meilisearch on publish webhooks.
WHY: Catalog 20 synthesizes the modern reference architecture for search optimization, content management, analytics compliance, and digital commerce. It establishes the foundational architectural boundary between marketing content and transactional commerce (the Reference Pattern), solving critical synchronization bugs, pricing discrepancies, and overselling risks inherent in duplicated catalogs. Furthermore, it codifies regulatory compliance workflows (GDPR/ePrivacy CMP prior-blocking), provides concrete trade-offs between monolithic systems (WordPress, WooCommerce) and headless compositions (Sanity + Shopify, Strapi + Medusa), and defines robust caching protocols separating long-lived editorial content from short-lived, price-sensitive commerce data.
WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not duplicate product pricing, discount logic, or stock levels into the CMS; always store handles/IDs and resolve live values from the commerce backend. Do not rely on client-side calculations for cart totals, shipping rates, or taxes; all payment intents and checkouts must be computed authoritatively on the server. Do not assume robots.txt directives provide access control; robots.txt only guides crawler discovery, so private routes and preview deployments must be protected by server-side authentication and noindex headers. Do not include private or preview URLs in sitemap.xml files. Do not fire analytics, session replay (PostHog), or marketing tags before user consent is confirmed in jurisdictions requiring opt-in compliance (EEA/UK); never initialize session replay without masking sensitive form inputs (passwords, PII, payment details). Do not run client-side JavaScript DOM-swapping A/B experiments that cause visual layout shifts (CLS regressions) or risk SEO cloaking penalties; enforce server/edge bucketing and exclude search bots. Do not bake unvalidated WordPress plugins into production without a strict update and patching cadence, and disable XML-RPC and theme/plugin file editing in wp-config.php. Do not expose Stripe secret keys, Resend API keys, or CMS write tokens in client-side bundles or source code. Do not deploy Medusa or Saleor without a dedicated operations plan for database clustering, Redis caching, search maintenance, and PCI DSS compliance scope.

Content caching longevity versus commerce pricing freshness: Marketing and editorial content benefits from long-term CDN caching with on-demand webhook invalidation (revalidateTag), whereas transactional commerce data requires ultra-short caching (<60s) or real-time server fetches to reflect live inventory and currency fluctuations.

Monolithic simplicity versus headless composability: Monolithic architectures (WordPress, WooCommerce, standard Shopify) offer rapid time-to-market and low infrastructure overhead (~$60–$150/year) for low-velocity content, whereas headless composable stacks (Sanity + Shopify + Next.js, Strapi + Medusa) yield superior developer experience and sub-1.5s Core Web Vitals at the cost of higher operational overhead (~$250–$3500/month) and multi-vendor coordination.

SaaS commerce convenience versus open-source self-hosted operational liability: Managed commerce platforms (Shopify) abstract PCI compliance, global scaling, and hosting at the price of recurring transaction fees (1.5–2% + monthly tiers), whereas open-source headless alternatives (Medusa, Saleor) eliminate platform fees but transfer full database, cache, security patching, and PCI SAQ scope to engineering teams.

HOW_TO_USE: 1. Scaffold React 3D scenes with R3F and Drei: Install "three", "@react-three/fiber", and "@react-three/drei"; lock peer dependencies (e.g. three >=0.156 with R3F v8, React 18/19); wrap scenes in declarative <Canvas> with OrbitControls and Environment staging.

2. Configure WebGPU renderers for modern compute pipelines: When using WebGPU-first libraries (Three-VFX, threeparticles), ensure three >=0.160 is installed, initialize WebGPURenderer, and supply async gl prop patterns to the R3F <Canvas>.

3. Chain postprocessing passes efficiently: Use "@react-three/postprocessing" and "postprocessing" EffectPass chains; enable MSAA by default on WebGL2; gate expensive passes (Bloom, MotionBlur) on mobile devices to protect GPU frame budgets.

4. Implement GPGPU particle simulations via FBO ping-pong: Utilize double-buffered floating-point RGBA textures (Nearest filtering) to store particle positions and velocities across simulation and render shader passes.

5. Extrude SVG and vector type safely: Parse vector outlines using opentype.js or SVG path loaders; apply ExtrudeGeometry with Z-offset ordering; audit font family licenses (SIL OFL, Apache) before distributing 3D type assets.

Do not run un-gated heavy postprocessing effects like bloom and motion blur on low-power mobile GPUs. Do not distribute extruded 3D typography without verifying the underlying font license (SIL OFL, Apache). Do not omit required attribution and Terms of Service compliance for map tile and data providers (OSM ODbL, Carto, Mapbox, Natural Earth). Do not neglect version-locking between three, @react-three/fiber, and @react-three/drei peer dependencies. conflicts: TypeScript 7.0 compiler port to Go (tsgo) drops the programmatic compiler API (ts.createProgram etc.), creating a hard incompatibility with typescript-eslint, ts-morph, and template-typecheckers, requiring those ecosystems to stay pinned to TypeScript 6.x until 7.1.

Node.js type-stripping implementation (amaro) evaluated and explicitly rejected tsgo as its transpile engine due to lack of blank-spacing mode and binary distribution overhead, maintaining SWC as its dependency.

Default package manager script security changed across Node 24 (npm 11.19+ skips install scripts by default via allowScripts) and pnpm 10/11 (strictDepBuilds / allowBuilds), breaking legacy packages relying on unvetted postinstall steps.

Ecosystem deprecation handoffs: Astral Rye is deprecated in favor of uv; egoist/tsup is in maintenance mode with author directing users to rolldown/tsdown; Volta maintainers have stood down with mise recommended as successor.
ts-node ESM loader compatibility broke on Node.js 20+ due to Node loader hook redesigns, requiring projects to transition to tsx (esbuild) or Node native type stripping.

Supply chain detection gap: standard advisory scanners (npm audit, pip-audit, osv-scanner) rely exclusively on published vulnerability registries and provide 0-day blind spots against account hijacks (e.g. March 2026 axios incident), necessitating behavioral analysis (Socket.dev) or release age cooldowns.

WHAT: Recommendation and Ranking Systems in Production Products (Domain B, Area 4): classical three-stage recommender funnel (candidate retrieval ~10ms via two-tower embeddings and ANN search -> heavy multi-objective neural ranking ~30ms -> business-rule reranking and diversity enforcement ~10ms within a 50-100ms total budget); deep case study of Netflix (multi-retriever fan-out, multi-objective completion/satisfaction scoring, experimentation infrastructure worth >$1B/year in retention); YouTube and TikTok architectures; and the transition to LLM-native rankers (Netflix GenRec 2026, using domain-adapted foundation models in vLLM prefill-only mode to score items strictly within a closed catalog, preventing out-of-catalog hallucinations while matching production quality with fewer labels).

Personalized e-commerce recommendations
Multi-objective engagement optimization

WHY: Provides the foundational engineering architecture for personalized discovery, demonstrating how to achieve sub-100ms latency at massive catalog scale and how to safely incorporate generative models into ranking without hallucination risks.
WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not score raw catalog items with unconstrained generative models. Do not optimize recommenders solely for click probability. Do not attempt single-stage ranking over large item catalogs. Do not ignore cold-start fallbacks for new users or fresh items.

HARNESS_WIRING.universal_note: Recommender systems must operate via multi-stage funnels within latency budgets; LLM rankers must be constrained strictly to scoring closed catalog IDs.

WHAT: Tool-Using and Autonomous Systems as Products (Domain B, Area 7): compounding failure mathematics across multi-step execution (Sierra tau-bench showing GPT-4o drops from 61% single-trial success to ~25% across an 8-trial session; Salesforce MCP-Universe showing 43.7% multi-tool success); five predictable tool-call failure modes (execution failure, malformed arguments, hallucinated tool names, timeouts, unexpected output volume); the boundary-layer principle (auth, retries, and secrets kept strictly in the API-client layer outside the model); real incidents ($63 / 31M-token runaway overnight loop); reference architecture for high-stakes agents (Polly Harness 9-layer system with approval interrupts and 229-case eval); layered guardrail doctrine (control outside the LLM, deterministic transaction limits, isolation, iteration caps); and MCP-era attack surfaces (EchoLeak CVE-2025-32711, Supabase/Cursor injection, OpenClaw supply chain poisoning).

WHAT: Inference Economics, Latency Budgets, and Reliability Engineering (Domain B, Area 9): cost drivers of LLM applications (compounding turn history, agent loop multiplication, long-context RAG); the 9-technique cost optimization stack ordered by implementation complexity (prompt prefix caching 60-90% savings, batch APIs 50%, output length constraints 15-30%, model routing 40-70%, semantic caching 31-47%, context compression 20-40%, quantization 30-60%, narrow OSS models 70-95%, distillation); the golden optimization sequence (instrument first, then cache, then route, then substitute); latency budgets per product surface (voice <800ms, chat 2-4s, RAG <2s, recommender 50-200ms); TTFT vs TPOT metrics; and the production reliability stack (deterministic validation, defined fallback chains, API circuit breakers, iteration caps, and four-pillar monitoring of quality, performance, cost, and reliability).

WHAT: Phase 8 Task 3 architectural disambiguation and reference implementation for the Definition of Done (DoD) pre-commit hook: compares Option A (native Git .git/hooks/pre-commit shell script) against Option B (OpenCode plugin hook tool.execute.before in .opencode/plugins/dod-gate.ts); establishes a dual-layer enforcement model where the native Git pre-commit script acts as the authoritative hard, tool-agnostic gate (blocking any commit from terminal, IDE, or agent if active feature in feature_list.json is in_progress or blocked) while the OpenCode plugin hook acts as an in-session soft early warning to prevent aborted commit tool calls before hitting git failure.
WHERE_USED: .git/hooks/pre-commit: native git commit hook at project root
.opencode/plugins/dod-gate.ts: OpenCode plugin hook for in-session interception
walkinglabs harness Definition of Done (DoD) gate enforcing feature_list.json passing status
CI and local terminal workflows preventing unverified code commits
HOW_TO_USE: Primary hard gate: Install executable bash script at .git/hooks/pre-commit (chmod +x); script reads feature_list.json via Node.js, checks for active features with status in_progress or blocked, and exits 1 with explanatory message if found (overrideable only via explicit git commit --no-verify)

Secondary soft gate: Create OpenCode plugin at .opencode/plugins/dod-gate.ts implementing tool.execute.before to intercept bash tool calls containing git commit, check feature_list.json, and return {abort: true, message: ...} before commit execution
Pass commits silently if feature_list.json does not exist or if all features are passing or not_started
In solo developer contexts, keep the hook fast (sub-second JSON parse, not a full test suite run) so flow is not interrupted
WHY: Protects repository integrity by ensuring that neither autonomous agents nor human developers can finalize git commits while an active feature remains unverified or blocked; provides defense-in-depth by pairing tool-agnostic Git enforcement (catches external/headless/manual commits) with agent-friendly session warning (catches errors early without crashing).
WHAT_NOT_TO_DO: Do not rely exclusively on the OpenCode plugin hook as the sole gate (OpenCode plugin hooks do not fire in manual terminal commits, external IDE commits, CI, or headless sessions); do not run full slow test suites inside the pre-commit hook (only inspect feature_list.json status to keep hook execution sub-second); do not remove the git commit --no-verify intentional override escape hatch; do not commit .git/hooks/pre-commit directly into git tracking (install via init.sh or setup script).
